perspective:
I, Harold Padilla, have access to the following information:

- I am a project manager. I know Arthur Begum as a police officer and a friend whom I rely on for advice and support.
- I felt frustrated and anxious because I believed my project team was unmotivated and that this was hurting progress. I arranged and attended a coffee-shop meeting with Arthur.
- I told Arthur my team seemed completely unmotivated and I was at my wit’s end. I heard him suggest understanding what drives each team member individually and having one-on-one conversations so people feel valued and understood. I agreed to try it, thanked him, and felt more hopeful.
- Afterward, I felt hopeful and relieved. I believed Arthur’s advice would help, so I told my team I wanted quick one-on-one chats to learn what motivates each of them. I heard Team Member 1 say that could be helpful and Team Member 2 say they were open to it. I said I would schedule time with each and wanted us to make the project a success together.
- I noticed the team still was not responding well to the new strategies. I felt disappointed and worried, then spoke with Arthur again. I told him the suggestions had not worked and I was worried about the project’s future. I heard him say there might be deeper team issues—personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors—and that I might need to dig deeper. I said I would set up another round of meetings.
- I felt determined and focused. I believed there might be underlying team issues I had not addressed. I held one-on-one meetings and asked team members to share concerns. I heard Team Member 1 report tension between a few people that was affecting work; I said I would look into resolving conflicts. I heard Team Member 2 report feeling overwhelmed by the workload and stressed; I said I would see about redistributing tasks and that their well-being mattered.
- I felt optimistic and empowered. I believed addressing individual concerns would improve team performance. I intended to create a more supportive, open environment through regular feedback sessions and team-building activities. I told the team this. I heard Team Member 1 say it sounded great and would help; Team Member 2 agreed and said it was good that concerns were being addressed. I said I was glad, wanted us to work together for project success, and that their input and well-being were crucial.

I do not have access to anyone’s unspoken thoughts, private motives, or narrator-only information beyond what I observed, heard, or was told.
